name: Iris Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on day shift this month, so the alarm goes at quarter past four and the bus to the pit leaves from outside the bakery on Copper Street at five. I drive a haul truck at the open-pit copper mine, the big ones that carry about 220 tonnes, and I've been on them a bit under two years, so I'm still the one the dispatcher watches. Most of the day is loading at the shovel, hauling up the ramp to the crusher, tipping, going back down, eleven or twelve hours of that.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cab at sunrise, honestly, when the whole pit goes orange and the radio's quiet. I like that it's a union site and the pay is real money for someone who left school at seventeen, even if I'm on the bottom rate. What wears me out is the vibration in my back and the feeling that I'm always one mistake from a write-up. And the north pit has six trucks that drive themselves now, on a trial, and nobody will tell us what the trial is for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, fine, back to work. At the union meeting I'd probably say it out loud, that all the scary talk was the company trying to keep us grateful for what we've got. Online I don't post much, but I'd share something from the union page saying so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, those six trucks in the north pit don't need some super AI. They're GPS and sensors and a control room, and they already work. So even if the big AI stuff is hype, I'm not sure my truck is safe. It just means it happens slower, a few trucks at a time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty much the same as now. Go to work, pay rent, keep going to the union meetings on the second Tuesday. I'd like to put money aside but there's nothing left over after rent and the car payment, so that's not really a plan, that's a wish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a little stone in my shoe. I'd sleep fine, but every time I drove past the north pit I'd look at those empty cabs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the trial trucks bother you even in a quiet world. What would you want the union to ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A straight answer, written down. How many trucks, by when, and what happens to the drivers. Marta, she's our delegate, asked at the last meeting and the site manager said the trial was about safety data, and everyone in the room laughed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If money's that tight even now, what's the first thing that goes when a month goes wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car payment, then I'd be in real trouble, because there's no other way out of town on a Sunday. So really it's food first. I already do the cheap shop at the discount place on the highway and bring my lunch in an old ice cream tub.

S0.say: I'd tell people the scary AI talk was mostly the company keeping us grateful and that I'm glad things stayed normal. At the union meeting I'd say it out loud and maybe share a post from the union page.
S0.think: I think the driverless trucks in the north pit don't need clever AI, they already work, so my job could still go a few trucks at a time. A quiet world just means it happens slower.
S0.do: Keeps working day shifts and going to the union meeting every second Tuesday. Wants to save but can't, because rent and the car payment take everything, so she keeps the cheap food shop going.
S0.feel: Mostly relief, with a small nagging worry every time she passes the empty cabs in the north pit.
S0.quote: Even if the big AI stuff is hype, I'm not sure my truck is safe. It just means it happens slower, a few trucks at a time.
S0.fieldNote: Even the calmest picture didn't fully settle her, because the threat she sees is the self-driving trial already running in the next pit. She separates fancy AI from plain automation, which is sharper than she gives herself credit for. Money is so tight that saving is a wish, not a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we have a union, and that if the company wants robots it has to share what it saves with the people it pushes out. I'd go to the meeting and I'd say that, even though I hate talking in front of the older guys. Online I'd share the petitions, all of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, haul trucks are the first thing to go. Drivers are the obvious cost, and I'm a junior driver with the worst safety record on my crew, two near misses on the ramp. If they cut twenty drivers, I'm in the twenty, I'm not stupid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to get a deal before the trucks come, like retraining paid by the company and no sackings without a payout. I'd stop the gym, cancel the streaming, and ask my landlord if I can pay fortnightly. Retraining on my own I wouldn't do yet, I don't even know what in, and I'm not going to sit at some computer course with no pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor is tilting slowly. I'd be angry more than scared, but the scared is underneath it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're 'in the twenty'. Who else on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Danny, who's fifty-two and has driven since before I was born, he can't read a screen without his glasses and he hates the new dispatch tablets. And me, really. We'd be the two names on the list for different reasons.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Some people in your spot would start learning the new systems so they stay on. Why not you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm bad at it, and I know it. They gave us tablets in the cab last year and it took me a month to stop pressing the wrong thing, the shift boss called me the fat-finger kid. I'd rather fight for the jobs than pretend I'm going to become a control room person.

S1.say: I'd say this is why we have a union and that if the company brings in robots it has to share the savings with the drivers it pushes out. I'd speak at the meeting and share every petition online.
S1.think: I think haul trucks go first and that a junior driver with two near misses will be on the list. If they cut twenty drivers, I expect to be one of them.
S1.do: Pushes the union to win paid retraining and payouts before the trucks arrive. Cancels the gym and streaming and asks her landlord about paying fortnightly, but holds off retraining herself because she doesn't know in what and can't study unpaid.
S1.feel: Angry on top and scared underneath, like the floor is slowly tilting.
S1.quote: If they cut twenty drivers, I'm in the twenty, I'm not stupid.
S1.fieldNote: Her public line is about the union and fair shares, but privately she's already put herself on the redundancy list. She resists learning the systems not out of pride but because she believes she's bad at screens. Collective action is where she puts her hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to stop it, or at least slow it down, and the people who own these machines should pay for everybody they replace. I'd be on the picket line if there was one. I'd write that online, even with my bad spelling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd be twenty-nine with no job, no savings and a car I can't pay off, in a town where the mine is the only big employer. There's a shop, a pub, the clinic and the mine. If the mine runs itself, the town runs out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd join every action going, the union, whatever protest there is in the city. I'd sell the car before they took it and move back into my mum's spare room two hours away, because rent is what kills me. Then I'd be in the queue for whatever the government sets up, if it sets anything up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like being in the cab when the brakes go soft on the ramp. That's the only way I can say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've had the brakes go soft on the ramp?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, my first winter. It was a sensor fault, not the brakes, but for about four seconds I thought I was going into the wall. That's what two years feels like, four seconds that don't end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum when you turned up with your bags?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her it's not forever, and she'd know I was lying. She cleaned at the clinic for twenty years and she'd be worried about her own job too, if robots are doing hands-on work. So really we'd be two people in one flat waiting to see who gets a payment first.

S2.say: I'd say the government has to slow it down and that the owners of the machines should pay for everyone they replace. I'd join any picket line and write about it online.
S2.think: I think in two years I'd be jobless with no savings in a town that only has the mine. If the mine runs itself, the whole town runs out of reasons to exist.
S2.do: Joins every union action and protest she can reach in the first months. Sells the car before it's repossessed, moves into her mum's spare room two hours away, and queues for whatever government support appears.
S2.feel: Like four seconds of brake failure on the ramp that never end.
S2.quote: If the mine runs itself, the town runs out.
S2.fieldNote: Two years leaves her no room at all, and she goes straight to the floor: car sold, back with her mum. Her image of the brake scare was vivid and clearly real for her. She also immediately saw her mother's cleaning job under threat, which doubles the fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, that it needs rules and the company and the tech people should pay into something for workers. But I'd say we've got time to fight properly, so I'd be pushing for that, a real campaign, not just being angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better than two, but I'd still be thirty-two with nothing, if I'm honest. Five years doesn't make me a different person. It just gives me longer to watch it coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to put a bit away every pay, even twenty a week into a separate account so I don't touch it. I'd stay active in the union and maybe stand for delegate when Marta steps down, so I'm in the room when they negotiate. I'd probably sign up for the heavy vehicle licence for road trucks, because at least that's driving and I know driving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, like a wet coat. Less like a crash and more like a long bad shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You just said road trucks. Wouldn't robots reach road trucks too in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah. You're right, they would. I said it because it's the only thing I know how to want. I guess I'd be buying myself a few years, not a future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what does the extra three years actually buy you, compared with the fast one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to not lose the car, maybe. Time for the union to get something on paper. And time to get used to the idea, which sounds small, but with the fast one I'd just be falling.

S3.say: I'd say it needs rules and that companies and tech firms should pay into something for workers. I'd say there's time to run a real campaign and that I want to be part of it.
S3.think: I think five years doesn't make me a different person and I'd still be in my thirties with nothing. It just gives me longer to watch it coming.
S3.do: Starts putting about twenty a week into a separate account and stays active in the union, aiming to stand for delegate. Considers a heavy vehicle road licence, while admitting robots would likely reach road trucks too.
S3.feel: Heavy and tired, like a long bad shift rather than a crash.
S3.quote: I said it because it's the only thing I know how to want.
S3.fieldNote: When I pointed out road trucks would be automated too, she accepted it at once, which was quietly sad. The extra time mainly buys her a chance to save a little and for the union to win something on paper. She wants to become a delegate, which is new and suggests the fight gives her a sense of control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this right, with the unions at the table and money for towns like ours. I'd say it at meetings and I'd vote for whoever promised that, which isn't always who I vote for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I can maybe live with. I'd be thirty-seven. That's young enough to start again if I had something to start with. It depends completely on whether anyone pays for that start, because I can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving, keep saving the twenty a week, and keep pushing the union. I'd probably finish the road licence and maybe a forklift ticket, small things I can do on weekends. If a company retraining scheme showed up, I'd take it even if I hated it, because ten years gives you time to be bad at something and get better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. It's the first one where I can picture myself on the other side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd take retraining even if you hated it. Earlier you said you'd rather fight than learn screens. What changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time changed it. If you give me ten years and somebody pays, I'll sit in the classroom. What I won't do is pay for it myself out of nothing and get told it's my fault I didn't keep up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the ten years came and nothing was done?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The owners and the government both. The owners because they'll have known for ten years and banked the savings. The government because their whole job is to see that kind of thing coming and they'd have spent it arguing.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, with unions at the table and support for mining towns. I'd vote for whoever promised that, even if it's not who I usually vote for.
S4.think: I think I could live with ten years because I'd be young enough to start again. It depends completely on whether someone pays for that start, because I can't.
S4.do: Keeps driving and saving about twenty a week while pushing the union. Finishes a road licence and a forklift ticket on weekends and says she'd take a company-paid retraining scheme even if she hated it.
S4.feel: Still worried, but she can breathe and picture herself on the other side.
S4.quote: Ten years gives you time to be bad at something and get better.
S4.fieldNote: The decade softened her stance on retraining, as long as someone else pays. Her blame is split evenly between owners and government. This was the first scenario where she could imagine a future, and her voice changed noticeably.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easy. There's nothing I could do in two years except lose things in the right order. What would help is a deal before the trucks come: a payout that's more than a few weeks, paid retraining with a wage while you do it, and somebody keeping the bus and the clinic open in towns like mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who's in the control room for those six trucks. It's three guys from head office in clean shirts who've never been down the ramp. Nobody's asking them if they're scared. Maybe they should be too.

headlineQuote: There's nothing I could do in two years except lose things in the right order.
portrait: Iris Fischer is a 27-year-old junior haul truck driver at a large open-pit copper mine who rents a room on Copper Street and lives payday to payday. She's a committed union member who struggles with in-cab screens and doesn't use AI tools. A self-driving truck trial in the next pit means she feels exposed even when AI fizzles, and in the faster pictures she puts her hope in collective action and expects to fall back on her mum. Only the ten-year picture lets her imagine retraining, and only if someone else pays.
biggestWorry: The AGI by 2028 picture, because in two years she'd have nothing to do except lose things in the right order.
whatWouldHelp: A deal before the trucks arrive: a real payout, retraining with a wage while she does it, and someone keeping the bus and clinic going in mining towns.
